title: Move around and look at things
objective: By the end of this lesson you can move anywhere in the filesystem and read every column of a detailed listing, including the parts most people skip.

blocks.text: Three commands do almost all of the moving and looking: pwd tells you where you are, ls shows what is here, and cd takes you somewhere else. The skill worth building is reading what ls tells you. Those columns answer security questions later.

blocks.caption: Moving around
lines: cd /var/log      # go to an absolute path
cd -             # go back to where I just was

blocks.text: The flags on ls that matter

rows: Long form: permissions, owner, size, modified time
Includes hidden entries — anything starting with a dot
Long form with human-readable sizes (4.0K instead of 4096)
Sorted by modification time, newest first

blocks.title: The combination to keep in your fingers
blocks.text: ls -lah — long form, hidden files included, readable sizes. Hidden files are where configuration lives, and they are exactly what an attacker would prefer you not to list.
Reading a long listing, column by column

items: -rw-r--r--  — the type and the permissions. The first character is the type: - is a regular file, d is a directory, l is a link
1 — how many names point at this same data
songpon — the user who owns it
staff — the group that owns it
Jul 31 14:02 — when it was last modified

blocks.text: You do not need to decode the permission characters yet — that is its own lesson. What matters now is knowing that the owner, the group, and those ten characters are all sitting there in every listing, waiting to be read.

blocks.title: Why the modified time is a security field
blocks.text: In an investigation, "which files changed around the time of the alert?" is one of the first questions. ls -lt sorts by exactly that. A configuration file in /etc with a modification time nobody can account for is worth explaining.

blocks.title: Read a real directory properly
steps: Find one entry whose name starts with a dot and note what it is
Look at the newest-modified configuration files on your machine
blocks.expected: Your home directory including hidden config files, then the most recently changed files in /etc. On a fresh machine the newest ones are usually from installation time.

blocks.title: When a command confuses you
blocks.text: Run man followed by the command name — for example man ls — to read its manual. Press q to quit. Man pages are what you fall back on when you are on a system you have never seen.

cheatsheet: pwd where am I · ls what is here · cd move
cd .. up one · cd home · cd - back to previous location
ls -lah is the workhorse: long form, hidden files, readable sizes
ls -l columns: type+permissions, links, owner, group, size, modified, name
First character: - file · d directory · l link
ls -lt sorts newest first — the investigation view
man <command> opens the manual; q quits

checkpoint.prompt: Which command shows hidden files with readable sizes and full detail?
checkpoint.explanation: -l gives the long form, -a includes dot-files, -h makes sizes readable. Together they are the listing you will use most.

checkpoint.prompt: In the listing line `drwxr-xr-x 2 songpon staff 4.0K Jul 31 14:02 reports`, what does the leading `d` tell you?

choices.A: The owner has disabled the file

checkpoint.explanation: The first character is the entry type: d for directory, - for a regular file, l for a symbolic link.

checkpoint.prompt: You are asked which configuration files changed most recently on a server. What do you run?
checkpoint.explanation: -t sorts by modification time, newest first. That question comes up constantly during incident work.
